items.question: For DeepWalk, what exact classification accuracy or F1 score was obtained on Flickr when the latent dimension was set to 128 and the number of walks per vertex was 30?
items.why_unanswerable: The passage discusses trends in performance with changing dimensionality and walk count, but it does not report any exact metric values for a specific setting like 128 dimensions and γ=30.
items.evidence_quote: Figures 5a1 and 5a3 examine the effects of varying the dimensionality and training rate.

items.question: How many labeled examples did DeepWalk use in the Flickr experiment at the 10% training-rate setting?
items.why_unanswerable: The passage compares 1% of Flickr to 10% of BlogCatalog in a relative way, but it never gives the exact number of labeled examples used for Flickr at 10%.
items.evidence_quote: (Note that 1% of Flickr has approximately as many labeled examples as 10% of BlogCatalog).

items.question: Under which hardware configuration did DeepWalk run the parameter sensitivity experiments on Flickr and BlogCatalog, including the GPU model and amount of memory?
items.why_unanswerable: The passage describes the experiments and parameter sweeps, but it gives no hardware or implementation environment details such as GPU type or memory size.
items.evidence_quote: In order to evaluate how changes to the parameterization of DeepWalk effect its performance on classification tasks, we conducted experiments on two multi-label classifications tasks (Flickr, and BlogCatalog).

items.question: Compared with DeepWalk using 30 walks per node, what was the percentage improvement from increasing the number of walks per vertex to 50 on BlogCatalog?
items.why_unanswerable: The passage says most of the benefit comes by starting with 30 walks per node, but it does not report a quantified improvement for 50 walks or any exact comparison percentage.
items.evidence_quote: The first is that there is most of the benefit is accomplished by starting γ = 30 walks per node in both graphs.
